data.content_ref: inline:The target's claim uses the word 'inevitably,' asserting that preference for corroborated theories necessarily smuggles in induction. Yet the target's own countercondition #3 — 'If acting on a theory does not involve any expectation of successful outcomes' — identifies a live escape route that the claim never closes off. The mechanism's load-bearing assertion that preferring a survived theory 'implies an expectation that it will continue to work' is a bare non sequitur. A methodological rule can rationally select the best-tested theory simply because all falsified alternatives have been eliminated and action is compulsory — a pragmatic, eliminative rationale that requires no inductive bridge from past survival to future success. Popper explicitly argued that corroboration is a past-tense report of severity of testing, not a predictor of future performance, and that acting on the best-tested theory is a policy choice among available options, not a belief in its probable truth. The target conflates pragmatic rationality (choosing the least-bad available option) with inductive inference (expecting future success), then declares the conflation 'inevitable' while simultaneously listing the disconfirming condition as a countercondition. A claim of inevitability that acknowledges a countercondition it fails to rule out is internally inconsistent.
